entries.meaning: Stands for a whole possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to her.”
examples: That desk by the window is hers.
My commute is forty minutes; hers is closer to ninety. (subject, singular referent — is)
Hers were the only comments the editor kept. (subject, plural referent — were)
She lent me a charger of hers and I never gave it back. (double genitive)
Take mine — hers is out of ink.
Isn't the gray coat hers? (question)
The mistake wasn't hers. (negative)
entries.pronunciation note: the weak form belongs to the double genitive — a friend of hers /ə frɛnd əv ɚz/, where the h drops entirely
entries.русский: её — принадлежащее ей, без существительного: «эта книга — её»; форма неизменяемая
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive)
entries.person / number: third person, singular possessor, female — or anyone referred to as she. Invariant: the form does not change with the number of the thing possessed (that book is hers, those books are hers).
entries.refers to: something belonging to, produced by, or associated with a female person or animal already identified. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a cousin of hers), or inanimate (the blue one is hers); the possessor must be animate and definite. For a possessor of unknown or nonbinary gender, use theirs.
entries.agreement: carries no ending of its own. When hers is the subject, the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, not the possessor: Hers is on the table (one bag), Hers are on the table (several). When hers is a subject complement, the subject has already fixed the verb: The seats by the door are hers.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be hers — that desk is hers · hers [verb] — hers arrived first · [verb] hers — take hers · [preposition] hers — park next to hers · [noun] of hers — a colleague of hers · comparison — bigger than hers, the same as hers · coordination — hers and mine
entries.contrast: Her precedes a noun (her coat); hers stands alone (the coat is hers). ✗ her's is never correct — no possessive pronoun in English takes an apostrophe. Keep it apart from object her as well: I called her (object of a verb) versus That call was hers (possessive). Before an -ing form the determiner is required, not the pronoun: ✓ We appreciated her coming, ✗ We appreciated hers coming.
entries.see also: her (determiner), his, theirs, mine, his or hers, her's, our's, your's, their's, its'

entries.meaning: Stands for a whole possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to him.”
examples: The blue folder on the counter is his.
My handwriting is bad; his is worse.
His were the only signatures missing from the form. (plural referent — were)
She's an old teacher of his from middle school. (double genitive)
Which locker is his? (question)
That call was never his to make. (negative)
He swore the truck was his, but the title said otherwise.
entries.pronunciation note: as a pronoun it usually carries some stress and keeps its /h/; the weak form shows up in the double genitive — a friend of his /ə frɛnd əv ɪz/
entries.русский: его — принадлежащее ему, без существительного: «эта машина — его»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); identical in form to the possessive determiner
entries.person / number: third person, singular possessor, male — or anyone referred to as he. Invariant.
entries.refers to: something belonging to, produced by, or associated with a male person or animal already identified. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a student of his), or inanimate (the red truck is his).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: His is missing (one form), His are missing (several). As a subject complement it never drives the verb: Those tools are his.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be his — the blue folder is his · his [verb] — his came back marked up · [verb] his — bring his · [preposition] his — sit next to his · [noun] of his — an old teacher of his · comparison — worse than his · coordination — his and hers
entries.contrast: His is the one possessive whose determiner and pronoun are spelled the same, so the test is what follows it: a noun after it makes it a determiner (his car), nothing after it makes it a pronoun (the car is his). Compare her ~ hers, your ~ yours, our ~ ours, their ~ theirs, where the pronoun adds -s. Generic his for a person of unstated gender (Every applicant should sign his) was standard until the 1970s and now reads as dated in American writing; use theirs, or rewrite in the plural.
entries.see also: his (determiner), hers, theirs, its, his or hers, hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn

entries.meaning: The third-person non-personal possessive — one of the two places where the possessive-pronoun paradigm has a hole in it, the other being generic one's.
examples: The city has a rhythm all its own. (its own — the ordinary way English fills the empty slot)
Once the rumor started, it took on a life of its own. (of its own stands in for the impossible ✗ a life of its)
Each department manages a budget of its own.
The dog wagged its tail the whole way home. (determiner use, no apostrophe — the form that gets misspelled ✗ it's tail)
✗ That collar is its. — not English. Say That collar is the dog's.
✗ Our revenue is higher than its. — say than theirs, or than that company's.
✗ Its is the red bowl. → ✓ The dog's is the red bowl. (subject position — the repair is a noun genitive)
If it expands to it is or it has, it isn't its: It's been a long week, but The company lost its lease.

body: The ordinary possessive with a noun after it (its tail, its lease) is a determiner, and it is not catalogued here — it is a cross-reference into Possessive and genitive determiners, and it appears in the examples below only so it can be told apart from the pronoun. 2. The standalone pronoun slot, which English simply leaves empty: ✗ That collar is its is not a sentence anyone says, and comparisons come out as than theirs or than the company's.
examples: The city has a rhythm all its own. (its own — the ordinary way English fills the empty slot)
Once the rumor started, it took on a life of its own. (of its own stands in for the impossible ✗ a life of its)
Each department manages a budget of its own.
The dog wagged its tail the whole way home. (determiner use, no apostrophe — the form that gets misspelled ✗ it's tail)
✗ That collar is its. — not English. Say That collar is the dog's.
✗ Our revenue is higher than its. — say than theirs, or than that company's.
✗ Its is the red bowl. → ✓ The dog's is the red bowl. (subject position — the repair is a noun genitive)
If it expands to it is or it has, it isn't its: It's been a long week, but The company lost its lease.

entries.pronunciation note: like mine, whose, and thine, its never reduces, and it is pronounced exactly like it's, which is why the two are confused only in writing
entries.русский: его, её (о предмете, животном) — пустая клетка: самостоятельно почти не употребляется, вместо него its own
entries.register: neutral as a determiner; as a standalone pronoun, rare enough that most Americans hear it as an error
entries.type: possessive pronoun — the empty cell in the paradigm: grammars list the form, but it almost never stands alone
entries.person / number: third person singular, non-personal. Invariant.
entries.refers to: something belonging to a thing, place, animal of unstated sex, organization, or abstraction — never to a named person. Where the standalone slot is needed, English fills it with its own (a life of its own) or with a noun genitive (that bowl is the dog's).
entries.agreement: in practice there is nothing to agree with, because the independent form does not occur. Use one of the substitutes and the verb then follows the head noun: The dog's is the red bowl (singular), The dog's are in the hall (plural).
entries.pattern: ✗ [noun phrase] be its — not English · the substitutes: [noun] of its own — a life of its own; [noun] all its own — a character all its own; noun genitive — that collar is the dog's · determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — its [noun]
entries.contrast: Its versus it's is the most-corrected error in written English. Its is the possessive and never takes an apostrophe (the dog wagged its tail); it's is the contraction of it is or it has (it's raining, it's been a week). The test: if the word can be expanded to it is or it has, write it's; otherwise write its. The reason the error is so common is that every other possessive in English — John's, the company's, somebody else's — is built with an apostrophe, so the hand adds one by reflex; the personal possessives are precisely the forms that refuse it. And ✗ its' does not exist in English in any sense at all.
entries.see also: it's (not a possessive pronoun), its (determiner), one's own, theirs, the company's, it

entries.meaning: Stands for a whole possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to me.”
examples: That gray jacket is mine.
Mine is the one with the cracked screen. (subject, singular referent — is)
Mine are still in the dryer. (subject, plural referent — are)
He's a colleague of mine from the Denver office. (double genitive)
Your numbers and mine don't match. (coordination)
Which of these coats is mine? (question)
The fault was mine, not hers. (negative contrast)
What's mine is yours.
entries.pronunciation note: the determiner my reduces to /mə/ in ordinary speech, but mine keeps its full diphthong even unstressed
entries.русский: мой, моя, моё, мои — принадлежащее говорящему, без существительного: «это моё»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive)
entries.person / number: first person, singular possessor — always the speaker. Invariant: that seat is mine, those seats are mine.
entries.refers to: something belonging to, produced by, or associated with the speaker. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a friend of mine), or inanimate (the gray suitcase is mine).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, not with the speaker: Mine is still in the dryer (one shirt), Mine are still in the dryer (several). As a subject complement the subject fixes the verb: These are mine.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be mine — that jacket is mine · mine [verb] — mine came back damaged · [verb] mine — use mine · [preposition] mine — park behind mine · [noun] of mine — a colleague of mine · comparison — older than mine · coordination — yours and mine · fixed frame — what's mine is yours
entries.contrast: My comes before a noun, mine stands alone: my seat versus that seat is mine. Before an -ing form use the determiner: ✓ They objected to my leaving early, ✗ to mine leaving early. Prenominal mine (mine eyes, mine host) is the archaic shape of the determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary. ✗ mines is nonstandard — see mines. And in coordination the possessive keeps its own form: ✓ my wife's and mine, ✗ my wife and I's — delete the other conjunct and the error is obvious, since ✗ I's car is not English.
entries.see also: my (determiner), ours, yours, of mine (the double genitive), mines

entries.meaning: Stands for a whole possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to us.”
examples: The house on the corner is ours.
Ours is the blue one with the porch. (subject, singular referent — is)
Ours were delivered a day late. (subject, plural referent — were)
They're old neighbors of ours. (double genitive)
Their deadline is Friday; ours was yesterday.
Is this table ours or theirs? (question)
The decision was never ours to make. (negative)
entries.pronunciation note: in relaxed speech it flattens to /ɑrz/ and lands on top of hours, which is the one place ours gets misheard
entries.русский: наш, наша, наше, наши — принадлежащее нам, без существительного
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive)
entries.person / number: first person plural — a group that includes the speaker. Invariant. English does not distinguish an inclusive ours (yours and mine) from an exclusive one (my side's, not yours); only context does.
entries.refers to: something belonging to, produced by, or associated with the speaker's group — a family, a team, a company, a household. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, or uncountable.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, never with the plural possessor: Ours is the blue house (one house, singular verb, even though ours means several people), Ours were delivered late (several items).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be ours — the house on the corner is ours · ours [verb] — ours came in first · [verb] ours — take ours · [preposition] ours — next to ours · [noun] of ours — a neighbor of ours · comparison — newer than ours · coordination — theirs and ours
entries.contrast: Our precedes a noun, ours stands alone: our table versus the table is ours. ✗ our's is never correct. Because casual ours /ɑrz/ collides with hours, careless writing produces ✗ a friend of hours. Note also that ours cannot be used before a gerund: ✓ They resented our leaving, ✗ They resented ours leaving.
entries.see also: our (determiner), mine, yours, theirs, her's, our's, your's, their's, its'

entries.meaning: Stands for a whole possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to them.”
examples: The corner office is theirs.
Our numbers are up; theirs are flat. (subject, plural referent — are)
Theirs was the only bid that came in under budget. (subject, singular referent — was)
He's a client of theirs. (double genitive)
Somebody left a phone on the seat — I think it's theirs. (singular they, standard American usage)
Whose turn is it, ours or theirs? (question)
The mistake wasn't theirs. (negative)
entries.pronunciation note: homophonous with there's in ordinary American speech; the weak form turns up in the double genitive — a client of theirs
entries.русский: их — принадлежащее им; тж. об одном человеке неизвестного или небинарного пола
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive)
entries.person / number: third person. Either a plural possessor (the neighbors, the Smiths) or a singular person referred to as they. Singular they is standard American English, in speech and in edited prose — AP and Chicago both endorse it — and theirs is its possessive pronoun. Invariant.
entries.refers to: something belonging to two or more people, or to one person of unknown or nonbinary gender. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, or uncountable, human (a client of theirs) or inanimate (the corner office is theirs).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, not with the possessor: Theirs was the only bid under budget (one bid — singular verb, though theirs points at a whole company), Theirs are flat this quarter (several figures). Singular they takes a plural verb in its own clause (they are), and that has no effect at all on the verb that follows theirs.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be theirs — the corner office is theirs · theirs [verb] — theirs arrived first · [verb] theirs — use theirs · [preposition] theirs — parked beside theirs · [noun] of theirs — a client of theirs · comparison — flatter than theirs · coordination — ours and theirs
entries.contrast: Five spellings cluster here, in two sound groups. Theirs is the possessive pronoun (the car is theirs), and there's — there is or there has (there's a problem) — is its exact homophone, both of them /ðɛrz/. The other three are /ðɛr/, with no final /z/: they're (they are — they're late), the determiner their (their car), and the place word there. Only there's can be mistaken for this word by ear; the rest are confused on paper alone. Expand the contraction to test: if there is fits, it takes an apostrophe. ✗ their's is never correct. Against the determiner their: a noun after it makes it a determiner (their car), nothing after it makes it the pronoun (the car is theirs).
entries.see also: their (determiner), there's (not a possessive pronoun), they're (not a possessive pronoun), ours, his or hers, zirs, they

entries.meaning: Stands for a whole possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to you.”
examples: Is this seat yours?
My flight is at six; yours is at nine. (subject, singular referent — is)
Yours are the only comments I haven't read yet. (subject, plural referent — are)
She's a big fan of yours. (double genitive)
The choice is yours.
That coat isn't yours — check the label. (negative)
Sincerely yours, / Yours truly (fixed letter closings)
entries.pronunciation note: the weak form is what you actually hear in a friend of yours /ə frɛnd əv jɚz/
entries.русский: твой, ваш (твоя, ваше, ваши) — принадлежащее собеседнику, без существительного
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive)
entries.person / number: second person, singular or plural — one addressee or many, with no change in form. Regional Southern speech supplies a separate plural, y'all's.
entries.refers to: something belonging to, produced by, or associated with the person or people being addressed. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a fan of yours), or inanimate (this seat is yours).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Yours is at nine (one flight), Yours are the only comments left (several). As a subject complement it never drives the verb: These tickets are yours.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be yours — is this seat yours? · yours [verb] — yours came back first · [verb] yours — bring yours · [preposition] yours — next to yours · [noun] of yours — a fan of yours · comparison — later than yours · coordination — yours and mine · fixed closings — Yours truly, Sincerely yours
entries.contrast: Your precedes a noun, yours stands alone: your seat versus the seat is yours. ✗ your's is never correct, and ✗ you're seat confuses the possessive with the contraction of you are — expand it to test. Note the frozen letter closings Yours truly and Sincerely yours, and the jocular self-reference yours truly, which means me: Guess who got stuck cleaning up? Yours truly.
entries.see also: your (determiner), mine, ours, y'all's, you're (not a possessive pronoun)

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the ae / aer set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to aer.”
examples: The gray suitcase by the door is aers.
My commute is forty minutes; aers is closer to ninety. (subject, singular referent — is)
Aers were the only comments the editor kept. (subject, plural referent — were)
She's an old colleague of aers from the Denver office. (double genitive)
Which locker is aers? (question)
The mistake wasn't aers. (negative)
Clip your form to the board next to aers. (object of a preposition)
Said aloud, aers and eirs are the same word; written down, each belongs to its own set. (the homophone problem)
entries.pronunciation note: the set is introduced as “ae like the letter, aer like air,” which makes the possessive a homophone of airs, of heirs, and of eirs
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — самостоятельная притяжательная форма набора ae/aer
entries.register: limited and rare. A twenty-first-century online coinage; an American meets it in pronoun introductions, profiles, email signatures, and fan writing, and effectively never in edited prose. Singular theirs is vastly commoner in every one of those settings.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the ae / aer set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ae (subject), aer (object), aer (determiner), aers (pronoun), aerself (reflexive). Invariant: the form does not change with the number of the thing possessed.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ae / aer for themselves — human only, and never a group. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a colleague of aers), or inanimate (the gray suitcase is aers).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, not with the possessor: Aers is on the table (one bag), Aers are on the table (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — ae is, ae has — where singular they takes are; that difference stops at the clause boundary and has no effect on the verb after aers.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be aers — the gray suitcase is aers · aers [verb] — aers arrived first · [verb] aers — take aers · [preposition] aers — park next to aers · [noun] of aers — a colleague of aers · comparison — older than aers · coordination — aers and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — aer [noun]
entries.contrast: Aer precedes a noun, aers stands alone — the same split as their ~ theirs. No apostrophe: ✗ aer's, for the same reason ✗ their's is wrong. Said aloud, aers and eirs are one word, and both of them sound like airs and heirs; on paper they are separate things belonging to separate sets, which is why a writer using either one glosses it at first mention. Against faers, which is built the same way on a different stem.
entries.variants: aer used as the independent possessive as well as the determiner, on the pattern of his, in which case the set is listed ae / aer / aer / aerself with no separate aers at all.
entries.see also: eirs, faers, zirs, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The genitive of the co set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to co.”
examples: The blue bicycle in the shed is cos.
Cos is the small room at the top of the stairs. (subject, singular referent — is)
Cos were the only hours nobody wanted on the schedule. (subject, plural referent — were)
She's an old neighbor of cos from the farm. (double genitive)
Which shift is cos this week? (question)
The decision was never cos to make. (negative)
Leave the tools on the bench beside cos. (object of a preposition)
One form does both jobs: cos shift starts at six, and the shift after it is cos too. (determiner, then pronoun — the his pattern)
entries.pronunciation note: the vowel is the /oʊ/ of co-op and co-worker, not the /ɑ/ of cos lettuce or of the trigonometric cos
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма местоимения co (М. Орован, 1970)
entries.register: limited, and limited in a particular way. The co set is house usage in several American intentional communities — Twin Oaks in Virginia and the rest of the Federation of Egalitarian Communities — where it has been unremarkable since the 1970s and turns up in newsletters, work schedules, and ordinary conversation. Outside them an American is unlikely ever to meet it.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the genitive of the co set, coined by Mary Orovan in 1970
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs co (subject), co (object), cos (determiner and independent pronoun alike), coself (reflexive) — one of the shortest paradigms of any coined set, with a single genitive doing both jobs, exactly as his does. Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses co for themselves — human only, and never a group. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a neighbor of cos), or inanimate (the blue bicycle is cos).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Cos is in the shed (one bicycle), Cos are in the shed (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — co is, co has.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be cos — the blue bicycle is cos · cos [verb] — cos came back first · [verb] cos — take cos · [preposition] cos — park next to cos · [noun] of cos — a neighbor of cos · comparison — newer than cos · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — cos [noun] — cos shift, cos room
entries.contrast: This is the one set in the section where the slot test changes nothing, because a single form fills both slots: cos bicycle and the bicycle is cos are both cos, the way his car and the car is his are both his. No apostrophe: ✗ co's — which matters more here than elsewhere, since co's would read as the contraction of co is. Three unrelated words share the spelling — the trigonometric cos /kɑs/, the cos of cos lettuce /kɑs/, and British cos meaning because /kəz/ — and none of them is a pronoun.
entries.variants: some listings give the object form as cos rather than co, making the set co / cos / cos / coself; ✗ co's is written for the possessive by people unfamiliar with the paradigm, which takes no apostrophe anywhere.
entries.see also: pers, thons, aers, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the ey / em / eir set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to em.”
examples: The corner desk by the window is eirs.
My commute is forty minutes; eirs is closer to ninety. (subject, singular referent — is)
Eirs were the only comments the editor kept. (subject, plural referent — were)
She's an old colleague of eirs from the Denver office. (double genitive)
Which locker is eirs? (question)
The mistake wasn't eirs. (negative)
Clip your form to the board next to eirs. (object of a preposition)
✗ Eir's is the one with the cracked screen. → ✓ Eirs is the one with the cracked screen. (no possessive pronoun in English takes an apostrophe)
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of airs and heirs; unstressed inside a phrase it drifts toward /ɚz/, which is where unstressed hers and theirs also land, so a friend of eirs is hard to place by ear alone
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора ey/em/eir (местоимения Спивака)
entries.register: limited. In circulation since the mid-1970s and 1980s, and an American meets it in online writing, in some science fiction and academic prose, and in pronoun introductions; it is far rarer than singular theirs.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the ey / em / eir set, usually called the Spivak pronouns
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ey (subject), em (object), eir (determiner), eirs (pronoun), emself (reflexive) — they / them / their / theirs / themself with the th- clipped off the front. Invariant: the form does not change with the number of the thing possessed.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ey / em / eir for themselves — human only, and never a group. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a cousin of eirs), or inanimate (the blue folder is eirs).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, exactly as with hers and theirs: Eirs is on the table (one bag), Eirs are on the table (several). In its own clause the subject form ey normally takes singular agreement — ey is, ey has — where singular they takes are; usage there is not fully settled, and none of it touches the verb after eirs.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be eirs — the corner desk is eirs · eirs [verb] — eirs arrived first · [verb] eirs — take eirs · [preposition] eirs — park next to eirs · [noun] of eirs — a colleague of eirs · comparison — older than eirs · coordination — eirs and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — eir [noun]
entries.contrast: Eir precedes a noun, eirs stands alone — the same split as their ~ theirs, which is precisely where the pair comes from. It takes no apostrophe: ✗ eir's, for the same reason ✗ their's is wrong. On paper the commonest difficulty is that a reader who has not met the form takes it for a typo for theirs or heirs, which is why a gloss at first mention earns its space. Against zirs and xyrs the difference is which set a person uses, not what the word means.
entries.variants: E, Em, Eir, Eirs, Emself with initial capitals — Michael Spivak's spelling, which is why the whole set is known as the Spivak pronouns; the lowercase ey / em / eir spelling is Christine Elverson's, formed by clipping they / them / their. Both are current, and eirs is the independent possessive in either.
entries.see also: theirs, zirs, xyrs, hirs, possessive and genitive determiners, they

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the fae / faer set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to faer.”
examples: The corner office at the end of the hall is faers.
My handwriting is bad; faers is worse. (subject, singular referent — is)
Faers were the only drawings that survived the move. (subject, plural referent — were)
He's a cousin of faers from out of state. (double genitive)
Is the gray coat faers or mine? (question)
That call was never faers to make. (negative)
Park behind faers and leave the hydrant clear. (object of a preposition)
Out loud it is fairs, fares, and faers all at once, so the word is glossed at first mention and the sentence built to carry it. (the homophone problem)
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of fairs and fares; the set is usually introduced as “fae rhymes with day, faer with air”
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора fae/faer, от fae «фея»
entries.register: limited and rare. A twenty-first-century online coinage built on the word fae (fairy), which puts it at the edge of the nounself pronouns — sets taken from a noun a person identifies with rather than from an existing pronoun. An American meets it in pronoun introductions, profiles, and fan writing, and effectively never in edited prose.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the fae / faer set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs fae (subject), faer (object), faer (determiner), faers (pronoun), faerself (reflexive). Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses fae / faer for themselves — human only, and never a group. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a cousin of faers), or inanimate (the corner office is faers).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Faers is on the table (one), Faers are on the table (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — fae is, fae has.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be faers — the corner office is faers · faers [verb] — faers arrived first · [verb] faers — use faers · [preposition] faers — parked beside faers · [noun] of faers — a cousin of faers · comparison — bigger than faers · coordination — faers and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — faer [noun]
entries.contrast: Faer precedes a noun, faers stands alone. No apostrophe: ✗ faer's. The practical difficulty is the homophony with the ordinary nouns fairs and fares — the tickets are faers has to earn its reading from context, and a reader meeting the word cold will hear the fairground or the bus. Against aers, the same shape without the f-, belonging to a different set.
entries.variants: fae / faer / faers / faerself is the standard listing; faeself is also found in the reflexive slot, and the subject form is occasionally spelled fey.
entries.see also: aers, zirs, eirs, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the ze / hir set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to hir.”
examples: The gray suitcase by the door is hirs.
Hirs is the one with the cracked screen. (subject, singular referent — is)
Hirs were the only signatures missing from the form. (subject, plural referent — were)
He's an old teacher of hirs from middle school. (double genitive)
Is the blue coat hirs or mine? (question)
That call was never hirs to make. (negative)
Park behind hirs and leave the hydrant clear. (object of a preposition)
Hirs and mine came back on the same day. (coordination)
entries.pronunciation note: the commoner reading rhymes with hears; speakers who say /hɝz/ make it a perfect homophone of hers, and only the spelling then keeps the two apart
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма наборов ze/hir и sie/hir
entries.register: limited. It belongs chiefly to the 1990s and 2000s wave of coinages, and an American meets it in writing from that period, in academic and fan communities, and where a person states it for themselves; the ze / zir spelling and singular theirs are both commoner today.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the ze / hir and sie / hir sets
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ze, zie, or sie (subject), hir (object), hir (determiner), hirs (pronoun), hirself (reflexive). Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ze / hir for themselves — human only. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a cousin of hirs), or inanimate (the gray suitcase is hirs).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Hirs is in the drawer (one), Hirs are in the drawer (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — ze is, ze has — which has no bearing on the verb after hirs.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be hirs — the gray suitcase is hirs · hirs [verb] — hirs came back marked up · [verb] hirs — bring hirs · [preposition] hirs — sit next to hirs · [noun] of hirs — an old teacher of hirs · comparison — worse than hirs · coordination — hirs and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — hir [noun]
entries.contrast: Hir precedes a noun, hirs stands alone — but this set is the one that blurs that line, because many users write hir in the independent slot too, on the pattern of his, which does both jobs. That desk is hir and that desk is hirs are both attested; hirs is the regularized form, built with the -s of hers, ours, and theirs. No apostrophe: ✗ hir's. The practical difficulty is the near-collision with hers — identical in speech for many speakers, one letter apart on paper — which is why hirs is easy to lose to a spell-checker.
entries.variants: hir used as the independent possessive as well as the determiner; the subject form appears as ze, zie, and sie, all of them taking the same hir / hirs.
entries.see also: zirs, hers, theirs, eirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The formal coordination that stands in for a single possessor of unstated gender — “the one belonging to him, or to her.”
examples: The last locker in the row is his or hers, not mine. (subject complement)
His or hers is the only signature still missing from the form. (subject, singular referent — is)
His or hers were the only forms returned on time. (subject, plural referent — were)
Every applicant submits a transcript, and his or hers has to reach us by Friday.
A juror may not discuss the case with a spouse of his or hers. (double genitive — and a fair sample of the clumsiness that drove the phrase out of use)
Is that badge his or hers? (question)
The error was not his or hers. (negative)
Rewritten the way an American editor would do it today: Theirs is the only signature still missing.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress lands on hers; unstressed, the h of his drops entirely, exactly as it does in a friend of his
entries.русский: его или её — книжн., устар.: о лице неуказанного пола; сегодня вытеснено theirs
entries.register: formal and dated. The house solution of American edited prose from roughly the late 1970s through the 1990s, when it was the standard repair for generic his; an American still meets it in contracts, employee handbooks, insurance policies, and statutes drafted in those decades. Singular theirs has since replaced it almost everywhere.
entries.type: coordinated possessive pronoun (independent genitive) — the standalone counterpart of the determiner his or her
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender unspecified. Never for a plural possessor — ✗ the employees … his or hers takes theirs — and, because the phrase names exactly two possibilities, not the form to use for a person who has stated they or a neopronoun.
entries.refers to: one unidentified person of unstated or irrelevant gender — the each employee, every applicant, a juror of institutional prose. Human only. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, or uncountable.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: His or hers is the only signature missing (one signature), His or hers were the only forms returned (several). Separately, the antecedent that licenses the phrase is grammatically singular and takes a singular verb of its own: ✓ Each employee is responsible for his or hers, ✗ Each employee are responsible for his or hers.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be his or hers — the last locker is his or hers · his or hers [verb] — his or hers is missing · [verb] his or hers — use his or hers · [preposition] his or hers — file it with his or hers · comparison — later than his or hers · the determiner, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — his or her [noun]
entries.contrast: Against singular theirs, which is shorter, standard, endorsed by AP and Chicago, and covers a person who uses they — which a phrase naming two options cannot. Against generic his (every applicant should sign his), which is dated in the other direction. In practice the best repair is usually neither one: make the noun plural — All employees are responsible for their own equipment. Note also that both halves have to be the independent forms: ✓ his or hers, and ✗ his or her with nothing after it, which is the determiner left stranded. ✗ his or her's is wrong twice over.
entries.variants: his/hers, her or his, hers or his, and the three-way his, hers, or theirs; the matching determiners are his or her, his/her, and her or his.
entries.see also: his or her (determiner), theirs, his, hers, one's (determiner)

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the ne / nem / nir set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to nem.”
examples: The red truck in the driveway is nirs.
Our numbers are up; nirs are flat. (subject, plural referent — are)
Nirs was the only bid that came in under budget. (subject, singular referent — was)
He's a client of nirs. (double genitive)
Whose turn is it, ours or nirs? (question)
The mistake wasn't nirs. (negative)
Leave your badge on the hook next to nirs. (object of a preposition)
Both spellings of the set — ne / nem / nir and ni / nir — give the same nirs here, so the form alone does not identify the paradigm.
entries.pronunciation note: the commoner reading rhymes with nears; the second lands on the vowel of her
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора ne/nem/nir
entries.register: limited and rare. One of the sets that circulate in online pronoun listings, profiles, and occasional fiction; an American meets it chiefly in pronoun introductions, and singular theirs is far commoner in all of them.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the ne / nem / nir set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ne (subject), nem (object), nir (determiner), nirs (pronoun), nemself (reflexive) — the ey / em / eir set with an initial n- on each form, both of them built on the model of they / them / their / theirs / themself. Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ne / nem / nir for themselves — human only, and never a group. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a client of nirs), or inanimate (the red truck is nirs).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Nirs was the only bid under budget (one bid), Nirs are flat this quarter (several figures). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — ne is, ne has — unlike singular they, which takes are.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be nirs — the red truck is nirs · nirs [verb] — nirs came in first · [verb] nirs — bring nirs · [preposition] nirs — sit next to nirs · [noun] of nirs — a client of nirs · comparison — worse than nirs · coordination — nirs and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — nir [noun]
entries.contrast: Nir precedes a noun, nirs stands alone — the same split as their ~ theirs, which is where the pair comes from. No apostrophe: ✗ nir's. The set is easy to mis-cite, because two spellings share the same genitive: ne / nem / nir / nirs and ni / nir / nirs differ in the subject and object slots and agree in this one, so nirs alone does not tell a reader which paradigm is in use.
entries.variants: ni / nir / nirs / nirself, a variant spelling of the same set that keeps nirs in this slot; the reflexive is written both nemself and nirself.
entries.see also: eirs, zirs, xyrs, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the per set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to per.”
examples: The red truck in the driveway is pers.
Pers is the small desk by the window. (subject, singular referent — is)
Pers were the only drawings that survived the move. (subject, plural referent — were)
She's an old neighbor of pers from the co-op. (double genitive)
Which of these coats is pers? (question)
The decision was never pers to make. (negative)
Set the box down beside pers. (object of a preposition)
Note the two words that look alike: the mileage is figured per day, and the truck is pers. (the Latin preposition against the pronoun)
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of purrs; the vowel is the one in her, not the one in pear
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора per (от person)
entries.register: limited and rare. An American meets it chiefly in feminist science fiction — Marge Piercy's Woman on the Edge of Time (1976) is where the set entered general circulation — and occasionally where a person states it for themselves.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the per set, clipped from person
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs per (subject), per (object), per (determiner), pers (pronoun), perself (reflexive) — one form covering most of the paradigm, the way you does in standard English. Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses per for themselves — human only, which is the point of a form clipped from person. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a cousin of pers), or inanimate (the red truck is pers).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Pers is on the table (one), Pers are on the table (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — per is, per has.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be pers — the red truck is pers · pers [verb] — pers came in first · [verb] pers — take pers · [preposition] pers — next to pers · [noun] of pers — a neighbor of pers · comparison — newer than pers · coordination — pers and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — per [noun]
entries.contrast: Per precedes a noun, pers stands alone. The collision to watch is with the Latin preposition per — per diem, per capita, miles per hour, as per your email — a different word entirely that is never a possessive, and one that makes per coat readable two ways for a beat. Many listings give per rather than pers in the independent slot, on the pattern of his; pers is the regularized form, built with the -s of hers and theirs. No apostrophe: ✗ per's.
entries.variants: per used as the independent possessive as well as the determiner, in which case the set is listed simply as per / per / per / perself with no separate pers at all.
entries.see also: zirs, eirs, theirs, vers, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The genitive of thon, an 1884 American coinage — “the one, or the ones, belonging to thon.”
examples: The last locker in the row is thons, not mine.
Thons is the only signature still missing from the form. (subject, singular referent — is)
Thons were the only forms returned on time. (subject, plural referent — were)
Every applicant submits a transcript, and thons has to reach us by Friday. (the institutional sentence the word was coined for)
A juror may not discuss the case with a spouse of thons. (double genitive)
Is that badge thons? (question)
Rewritten the way an American would write it today: Theirs is the only signature still missing.
The th- is the th- of that one, which the word is blended from — not the th- of theirs.
entries.pronunciation note: the th is the voiced one of that, not the voiceless one of thin, because the word is a blend of that one
entries.русский: устар. — притяжательная форма thon, первого гендерно-нейтрального местоимения (1884)
entries.register: archaic. Coined in 1884 by Charles Crozat Converse, an American lawyer and hymn composer, carried in Funk & Wagnalls' Standard Dictionary from 1897 and in Merriam-Webster's New International of 1934, and dead in ordinary use by the middle of the twentieth century. An American meets it now in histories of the pronoun problem and nowhere else.
entries.type: possessive pronoun — the genitive of thon, the first gender-neutral pronoun to reach an American dictionary; determiner and independent pronoun alike
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs thon (subject and object alike), thons (determiner and pronoun alike), thonself (reflexive) — a three-form paradigm blended from that one. Invariant.
entries.refers to: one person of unstated, unknown, or irrelevant gender — the every applicant, each employee, a juror of institutional prose, which is exactly what Converse invented it for. Human only.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Thons is the signature still missing (one), Thons were returned late (several). The subject form took singular agreement in its own clause — thon is, thon has.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be thons — the last locker is thons · thons [verb] — thons is missing · [verb] thons — use thons · [noun] of thons — a colleague of thons · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — thons [noun] — thons signature
entries.contrast: Thons is the ancestor of everything else in this section: the earliest of the American gender-neutral coinages, the only one ever given a long run in a major dictionary, and the plain evidence that the problem is a century and a half old rather than a recent one. Against theirs, which solved the same problem with a word English already had, and against his or hers, which solved it by naming both options. Do not read the th- as the th- of theirs: the blend is that one, and the two words are unrelated.
entries.variants: thon's in some nineteenth-century printings; thon itself is occasionally given in the genitive slot, and the reflexive appears as thonself and as thon's self.
entries.see also: theirs, his or hers, cos, pers, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the ve / ver set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to ver.”
examples: The corner office is vers.
Our numbers are up; vers are flat. (subject, plural referent — are)
Vers was the only bid that came in under budget. (subject, singular referent — was)
He's a client of vers. (double genitive)
Whose turn is it, ours or vers? (question)
The mistake wasn't vers. (negative)
The truck parked beside vers has been there all week. (object of a preposition)
In Egan's paradigm the same sentence reads the corner office is vis, which is the other half of the split. (the competing shape of the set)
entries.pronunciation note: the vowel of her; a near-homophone of verse, differing only in the voicing of the last consonant
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора ve/ver (научная фантастика)
entries.register: limited and rare. The ve set is met mainly in science fiction — Greg Egan's novels are where most American readers have run into it — and in online pronoun listings.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the ve / ver set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ve (subject), ver (object), ver (determiner), vers (pronoun), verself (reflexive). Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ve / ver for themselves — human only. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a client of vers), or inanimate (the corner office is vers).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Vers was the only bid under budget (one bid), Vers are flat this quarter (several figures). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — ve is, ve has.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be vers — the corner office is vers · vers [verb] — vers arrived first · [verb] vers — use vers · [preposition] vers — parked beside vers · [noun] of vers — a client of vers · comparison — flatter than vers · coordination — ours and vers · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — ver [noun]
entries.contrast: Ver precedes a noun, vers stands alone. This is the one set in the file whose two shapes genuinely compete: ve / ver / vis / vis / verself builds the possessive as vis, on the model of his, and is the paradigm Greg Egan's fiction uses; ve / ver / vers / vers / verself builds it on ver with the regular -s, and vers is its independent form. A reader who has met one will not necessarily recognize the other, so the set is worth naming at first mention. No apostrophe: ✗ ver's.
entries.variants: vis, the possessive of the ve / ver / vis paradigm, which covers both the determiner and the pronoun (vis coat, the coat is vis); ver is also found in the determiner slot alongside vis.
entries.see also: pers, zirs, eirs, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the xe / xem / xyr set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to xem.”
examples: The blue folder on the counter is xyrs.
My handwriting is bad; xyrs is worse. (subject, singular referent — is)
Xyrs were the only comments the editor kept. (subject, plural referent — were)
She's an old student of xyrs from the seminar. (double genitive)
Which locker is xyrs? (question)
That call was never xyrs to make. (negative)
Leave your badge on the hook next to xyrs. (object of a preposition)
Said aloud, xyrs and zirs are the same word; written down, they are two, and each belongs to its own set. (the homophone problem)
entries.pronunciation note: the x spells /z/, so the word starts like zebra, not like ex
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора xe/xem/xyr
entries.register: limited. In American online writing since the 1990s, and now met mainly in pronoun introductions, profiles, email signatures, and class rosters; one of the more frequently listed neopronoun sets, alongside ze / zir and ey / em, and far rarer than singular theirs in every one of those settings.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the xe / xem / xyr set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs xe (subject), xem (object), xyr (determiner), xyrs (pronoun), xemself (reflexive). Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses xe / xem / xyr for themselves — human only. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a student of xyrs), or inanimate (the blue folder is xyrs).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed: Xyrs is missing (one form), Xyrs are missing (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — xe is, xe has — unlike singular they, which takes are.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be xyrs — the blue folder is xyrs · xyrs [verb] — xyrs came back marked up · [verb] xyrs — bring xyrs · [preposition] xyrs — sit next to xyrs · [noun] of xyrs — an old student of xyrs · comparison — worse than xyrs · coordination — xyrs and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — xyr [noun]
entries.contrast: Xyr precedes a noun, xyrs stands alone. Because x- here spells /z/, xyrs and zirs are homophones — the same word in speech, told apart only by which spelling tradition the writer is following, and not interchangeable on paper, since each belongs to its own set. No apostrophe: ✗ xyr's. The spelling is the practical difficulty: a reader meeting the form cold will try /ks/ or /ɛks/ at the front of it, which is why writers who use it often gloss the pronunciation once.
entries.variants: xirs, from the xe / xem / xir spelling of the same set; the set is also written ze / zem / zyr, in which case the independent possessive is zyrs.
entries.see also: zirs, eirs, hirs, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners

entries.meaning: The independent possessive of the ze / zir set — “the one, or the ones, belonging to zir.”
examples: The corner office is zirs.
My commute is forty minutes; zirs is closer to ninety. (subject, singular referent — is)
Zirs were the only comments the editor kept. (subject, plural referent — were)
He's a colleague of zirs from the Denver office. (double genitive)
Is the gray coat zirs? (question)
The mistake wasn't zirs. (negative)
Park behind zirs and leave room for the truck. (object of a preposition)
Take mine — zirs is out of ink. (coordination against another possessive)
entries.pronunciation note: a homophone of xyrs, which is the same word in a different spelling tradition
entries.русский: неологизм, русского эквивалента нет — притяжательная форма набора ze/zir
entries.register: limited. One of the more frequently used neopronoun sets in American English, met in pronoun introductions, email signatures, name badges, class rosters, and online profiles, chiefly among nonbinary and genderqueer speakers and the people writing about them. Singular theirs is far commoner in all of those settings.
entries.type: possessive pronoun (independent genitive); neopronoun — the independent possessive of the ze / zir set
entries.person / number: third person singular, gender-neutral. The set runs ze or zie (subject), zir (object), zir (determiner), zirs (pronoun), zirself (reflexive). Some speakers pair ze with hir instead — see hirs. Invariant.
entries.refers to: one specific person who uses ze / zir for themselves — human only, and never a group. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, uncountable, human (a colleague of zirs), or inanimate (the corner office is zirs).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the number of the thing possessed, never with the possessor: Zirs is on the table (one bag), Zirs are on the table (several). The subject form takes singular agreement in its own clause — ze is, ze has — unlike singular they, which takes are; that difference stops at the clause boundary and has no effect on the verb after zirs.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be zirs — the corner office is zirs · zirs [verb] — zirs arrived first · [verb] zirs — use zirs · [preposition] zirs — parked beside zirs · [noun] of zirs — a colleague of zirs · comparison — bigger than zirs · coordination — zirs and mine · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — zir [noun]
entries.contrast: Zir precedes a noun, zirs stands alone — though this set, like ze / hir, is often listed with zir doing both jobs on the pattern of his, so the coat is zir and the coat is zirs are both attested; zirs is the regularized independent form, built with the -s of hers, ours, and theirs. No apostrophe: ✗ zir's. Homophonous with xyrs — the two spellings belong to two different sets and are not interchangeable in writing.
entries.variants: zir used as the independent possessive as well as the determiner; the subject form is written ze and zie; and the ze / hir pairing gives hirs in this slot instead.
entries.see also: xyrs, hirs, eirs, theirs, possessive and genitive determiners, they

entries.meaning: Combines possession with an indefinite, demonstrative, or quantified determiner — the workaround for a noun phrase that has room for only one determiner.
examples: She's an old friend of mine from college. (a/an + singular countable)
That car of his has broken down three times this year. (demonstrative, and plainly not neutral)
Two cousins of hers flew in for the wedding. (number + plural countable)
Several clients of ours asked the same question. (quantifier + plural countable)
A painting of my father's hung over the mantel — he painted it. (compare a painting of my father, which would show him)
Is this book of theirs worth reading? (question)
I haven't met a single neighbor of yours. (negative)
entries.pronunciation note: of is nearly always the weak /əv/ or /ə/ here, which is why the phrase is sometimes written a friend o' mine
entries.русский: один из моих — двойной генитив: a friend of mine = один из моих друзей
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: construction — of plus a possessive pronoun; also called the oblique genitive or post-genitive
entries.person / number: any person and number — of mine, of yours, of his, of hers, of ours, of theirs, and with a genitive noun phrase of John's, of my sister's. There is no its form: ✗ a page of its → one of its pages.
entries.refers to: the possessor named by the pronoun. The head noun is normally countable — singular after a/an or a demonstrative (a friend of mine, that car of his), plural after a number or quantifier (two cousins of hers, several clients of ours). With an uncountable noun it is limited to demonstrative and evaluative uses: ✓ that attitude of yours, ✗ a money of mine.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the head noun, never with the possessor: A friend of mine is coming, Two friends of mine are coming, Several clients of ours have asked.
entries.pattern: [a/an / number / demonstrative / quantifier] [noun] of mine / yours / his / hers / ours / theirs · [same] [noun] of [name]'s — a friend of John's · with own — a place of her own
entries.contrast: It is not redundant, because English allows exactly one determiner in the central slot: ✗ a my friend and ✗ that your car are impossible, so the possessive gets pushed to the end. It also is not synonymous with a plain of-phrase — a picture of my father has him in it, while a picture of my father's belongs to him or was taken by him. With a demonstrative it usually carries an attitude: that car of yours is rarely neutral. And the complement of of must be a possessive pronoun or a genitive noun phrase — ✗ a friend of me, ✗ a friend of my are both wrong.
entries.see also: mine, hers, theirs, of mine (determiner dictionary), John's

entries.meaning: Names one further, unnamed possessor — “belonging to some other single person.”
examples: One person's freedom ends where another's begins.
The handwriting on the envelope wasn't hers; it was another's.
He signed at the bottom, and beneath his name was another's.
It is easy enough to bear one's own troubles and impossible to bear another's. (comparison)
She refused to take credit that was another's. (relative clause)
Whose fault was it — yours, or another's? (question)
The manuscript he was carrying turned out to be another's, borrowed and never returned.
✗ Anothers' is not a word: another is already singular, and the plural of the idea is others'.
entries.pronunciation note: the th is voiced, as in other; the first syllable is a bare schwa and drops out altogether in fast speech — 'nother's
entries.русский: другого, чужое — книжн.: принадлежащее иному лицу («свобода другого»)
entries.register: neutral as a determiner; the standalone pronoun use is formal, literary, and proverbial
entries.type: indefinite genitive pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular — another is an + other, so it can only ever name one further person. There is no ✗ anothers'; the plural of the same idea is others'.
entries.refers to: one further person, not the one already under discussion — human only, and normally left unidentified. The thing possessed is supplied by context, and in the commonest use it is the noun that has just appeared: one person's freedom ends where another's begins = where another person's freedom begins.
entries.agreement: the possessor is always singular — another can only ever be one further person, and there is no plural ✗ anothers'. The verb, as everywhere in this file, follows the understood possessed noun and not the possessor: Another's is the signature underneath (one signature), Another's are the gloves on the left (several), and where another's begins takes begins because the understood noun (freedom) is singular.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be another's — the handwriting was another's · [noun]'s … another's — one person's freedom … another's · comparison — his own troubles and another's · [noun] of another's — a manuscript of another's · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — another's [noun] — at another's expense
entries.contrast: Against others', the plural of the same idea — another's points at one further person, others' at several. Against one another's, which is reciprocal and points crosswise inside a group (they wore one another's coats), catalogued in Reflexive and reciprocal pronouns. And against the far commoner determiner use: a noun after it (another's problem, at another's expense) puts the phrase in the other dictionary. Note that another's is never a contraction — there is no short form of another is — so the apostrophe here is only ever a genitive, which is what makes it easier to read than anyone's or nobody's.
entries.see also: others', somebody else's, anyone's, each other's, another

entries.meaning: The else frame, which pushes the genitive ending onto else — “belonging to some other person than this one.”
examples: That coat isn't mine, and it isn't anyone else's on this floor.
My guess is as good as anyone else's.
Everyone else's is already in; yours is the last one we're waiting on. (subject, singular verb — is)
The decision was no one else's but the mayor's. (the negation is inside the phrase, so the verb stays positive)
Her schedule is packed, but so is everybody else's. (comparison, the -body stem)
He turned up in a jacket of someone else's that he'd found in the closet. (double genitive)
Whose problem is it now? Everyone else's. (short answer)
✗ Anyone's else → ✓ anyone else's: the ending goes on the end of the phrase, not on the pronoun.
entries.pronunciation note: the 's lands on else and comes out /ɪz/ after the /s/, exactly as in Chris's; the whole phrase carries one main stress, on else
entries.русский: чей-либо ещё, чужое — принадлежащее любому другому человеку
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: group genitive used as a pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular — the indefinite in front of else keeps its singular verb even where the sense takes in a whole group, so with the usual distributive singular understood, ✓ Everyone else's is different, ✗ Everyone else's are different. Where the understood possessed noun is itself plural, the verb follows it like any other fused genitive: Mine is short; everyone else's are longer. The frame is fully productive — anybody else's, everyone else's, everybody else's, no one else's, nobody else's, someone else's, who else's.
entries.refers to: a person other than the one already mentioned, human only. Which person depends on the indefinite in front of else: anyone else's opens it to anybody at all, everyone else's takes in all the others at once, no one else's shuts every other person out. The thing possessed comes from context.
entries.agreement: grammatically singular, like the indefinite it is built on: Anyone else's is better than nothing, Everyone else's is already in, No one else's was ready. With no one else's the verb stays positive, because the negation sits inside the phrase: ✓ The fault was no one else's, ✗ wasn't no one else's.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be anyone else's — that seat isn't anyone else's · comparison — as good as anyone else's, better than everyone else's · no one else's but [possessive] — no one else's but hers · [noun] of someone else's — a jacket of someone else's · short answer — Whose problem is it now? Everyone else's. · the frame — [indefinite pronoun] else's
entries.contrast: The ending goes on else, not on the indefinite, because the English genitive attaches to a whole phrase and else is what ends it: ✓ anyone else's, ✗ anyone's else. The same mechanism gives ✓ who else's against the impossible ✗ whose else. With a noun after it (anyone else's guess) the phrase is a determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary. Against bare anyone's: anyone's opens the field to everybody, the person in front of you included, while anyone else's deliberately shuts that person out.
entries.variants: anybody else's /ˌɛnibɑdi ˈɛlsɪz/ · en-ee-bah-dee EL-siz — the same phrase on the -body stem, identical in grammar and register and the commoner of the two in speech. Everyone else's and everybody else's, “belonging to all the other people.” No one else's and nobody else's, “belonging to no other person,” with the verb kept positive. Someone else's and somebody else's, catalogued separately at somebody else's. And who else's, the interrogative member of the frame.
entries.see also: somebody else's, anyone's, everyone's, nobody's, somebody else's (determiner), someone else's

entries.meaning: Names an unspecified possessor — “belonging to any person at all,” and by extension “up for grabs.”
examples: With two laps to go, the race was still anyone's.
My guess is as good as anyone's.
Nobody claimed the wallet, so it could be anybody's.
His chances are better than anyone's on that roster.
Whose signature is missing? At this point it could be anyone's.
Anyone's is better than nothing at this point. (subject, singular verb — is)
Don't go by mine — go by anyone's on the committee. (object of a preposition)
Anyone's welcome to try. (not the possessive — this is anyone is)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to the contraction anyone is; only context separates them
entries.русский: чей угодно — принадлежащее любому человеку; только о людях
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: indefinite genitive pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular in form, though it points at an open set of people. The same pattern runs through anybody's, someone's, everyone's, no one's.
entries.refers to: any person at all, human only; the thing possessed is supplied by context (the race is still anyone's = anyone's race). It cannot point at a thing — for a non-human possessor use a noun genitive (the company's).
entries.agreement: grammatically singular: Anyone's is better than nothing. When it is a subject complement the subject fixes the verb: The chances are anyone's.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be anyone's — the race is still anyone's · as good as anyone's · better than anyone's · [verb] anyone's — it could be anybody's · the else variant — anyone else's
entries.contrast: The apostrophe carries two different jobs here: Anyone's welcome to try is anyone is, while the decision is anyone's is the possessive. Expand it to tell them apart. Keep it apart from the determiner use as well — anyone's guess has a noun after it and belongs to the determiner dictionary. Note also anyone's (one indefinite person) against any one's (any single member of a stated set).
entries.variants: anybody's /ˈɛnibɑdiz/ · EN-ee-bah-deez — the same pronoun on the -body stem, identical in grammar, reference, and register, and the commoner of the two in speech, where anyone's is the commoner in writing. Also the else forms anyone else's and anybody else's, and the two-word any one's, which picks a single member out of a stated set.
entries.see also: everyone's, nobody's, somebody's, somebody else's, anyone

entries.meaning: Names the whole group as possessor — “belonging to every person in it,” and by extension “shared by all of us.”
examples: The credit was everyone's, not just the director's. (subject complement)
Everyone's is different — there's no single right answer. (subject, singular verb)
Whose problem is this? Everyone's. (short answer)
My schedule is packed, but so is everybody's. (comparison, the -body stem)
That call was never everyone's to make. (negative)
Is the courtyard everyone's, or just the ground-floor tenants'? (question)
Everyone's welcome to stay for dinner. (not the possessive — this is everyone is)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to the contraction everyone is; everybody's /ˈɛvribɑdiz/ behaves the same way in every respect
entries.русский: всех, каждого — принадлежащее всем сразу; только о людях
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: indefinite genitive pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular in form, though the sense takes in the whole group — everyone is, everybody is, never ✗ everyone are, and the genitive keeps that singular agreement. The same frame gives everybody's and everyone else's.
entries.refers to: every member of the group, human only; the thing possessed is supplied by context (the credit is everyone's = everyone's credit). For a non-human possessor use a noun genitive (the company's).
entries.agreement: grammatically singular, and it stays singular even though the meaning is collective: ✓ Everyone's is different, ✗ Everyone's are different. This is the same singular that governs everyone, everybody, someone, anyone, and nobody. The verb still answers to the understood possessed noun, so a plural one pulls it plural — Mine is short; everyone's are longer — but the distributive singular is the ordinary case, and it is the one the ✗ above rules out. When a pronoun refers back to it, standard American English uses singular they: Everyone's is different, and they all know it. As a subject complement the subject fixes the verb: The seats along the wall are everyone's.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be everyone's — the credit is everyone's · everyone's [verb] — everyone's is different · comparison — as bad as everyone's · short answer — Whose problem is it? Everyone's. · the else variant — everyone else's
entries.contrast: One spelling, two words: Everyone's here is everyone is here, while the responsibility is everyone's is the possessive — expand it to test. Everyone's guess has a noun after it and is a determiner, catalogued in the determiner dictionary. Against nobody's: everyone's spreads the ownership across the whole group, nobody's denies it to all of them, which is why the two pair off in everyone's and nobody's. Note also everyone's (the group as a whole) against every one's (each separate member of a stated set).
entries.variants: everybody's /ˈɛvribɑdiz/ · EV-ree-bah-deez — the same pronoun on the -body stem, identical in grammar, reference, and register, and the commoner of the two in speech; it keeps the same singular agreement (✓ Everybody's is different, ✗ Everybody's are different). Also the else forms everyone else's and everybody else's, and the two-word every one's, which picks out each separate member of a stated set.
entries.see also: anyone's, nobody's, somebody's, somebody else's, everyone

entries.meaning: A name plus 's, standing in for the whole possessive noun phrase — “the one belonging to John.”
examples: The blue car in the driveway is John's.
John's is the desk by the window. (subject, singular referent — is)
We're having dinner at John's tonight. (locative genitive — John's house)
She's a cousin of John's. (double genitive)
Both signatures were Maria's, not John's.
Is that mug John's or mine? (question)
John's was the only application filed on time.
entries.pronunciation note: the genitive 's is /s/ after a voiceless sound (Pat's), /z/ after a voiced one (John's), and /ɪz/ after a sibilant (Chris's) — the same three-way split as the plural
entries.русский: Джона — принадлежащее Джону; тж. «у Джона (дома)»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: genitive noun phrase used as a pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person; singular possessor here, but the construction is fully productive — any noun phrase, of any person or number, can do this.
entries.refers to: whatever the context supplies. Three readings: the possessed thing (the blue car is John's), a place associated with the possessor (dinner at John's = at his house), and the possessor himself inside a double genitive (a cousin of John's).
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the understood head noun, not with the possessor: John's is the desk by the window (one desk), John's are in the hall closet (several coats).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be John's · John's be [complement] — John's is the red one · [preposition] John's — at John's, to John's (his house) · [noun] of John's — a cousin of John's · the same frame with any noun phrase — Maria's, the doctor's, my sister's
entries.contrast: John's the genitive and John's the contraction of John is or John has are spelled identically: John's late is John is late; the car is John's is possession. Expand it to test. And keep the two dictionaries apart with the slot test: John's car has a noun after it and is a determiner; the car is John's has nothing after it and is a pronoun. The locative use (we're eating at John's) is the same fused genitive with house or place understood, and it is what lies behind store names like Macy's and Trader Joe's.
entries.see also: John's (determiner), the company's, the Smiths', of mine (the double genitive), 's (singular genitive)

entries.meaning: Names the absence of a possessor — “belonging to no one.”
examples: The strip of land behind the fence is nobody's.
Whose fault was it? Nobody's, really.
That bike has sat in the rack for two years — it must be nobody's.
The credit was everyone's and nobody's at the same time.
The decision was no one's but the mayor's.
Nobody's was finished on time. (subject, singular verb — was)

The land is nobody's, not ✗ isn't nobody's — the negation is already inside the word. (double negative: ordinary in African American English and in Southern and working-class white vernaculars, nonstandard in edited prose)
Nobody's answering the phone. (not the possessive — this is nobody is)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to the contraction nobody is, as in nobody's home
entries.русский: ничей — никому не принадлежащий; только о людях как владельцах
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: indefinite genitive pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular. No one's is the same word in two words; none's does not exist.
entries.refers to: no person at all — it asserts that the thing has no owner. Human possessors only.
entries.agreement: grammatically singular, like the pronoun it is built on — nobody is, ✗ nobody are: ✓ Nobody's was finished on time. And the verb stays positive, because the negation is already inside the word: ✓ The land is nobody's, ✗ The land isn't nobody's. That second sentence is a double negative — not illogical, and entirely ordinary in African American English and in Southern and working-class white vernaculars, where the second negative intensifies rather than cancels — but it is nonstandard in edited American prose; see negative concord.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be nobody's — the strip of land is nobody's · nobody's but [possessive] — nobody's but hers · short answer — Whose fault was it? Nobody's. · the else variant — nobody else's
entries.contrast: Two words, one spelling. Nobody's home is nobody is home; the land is nobody's is the possessive. Expand it to test. The frozen phrases nobody's fool and nobody's business have a noun after them and are therefore determiners, not pronouns. Against anyone's: anyone's says the thing is open to all comers, nobody's says it belongs to none of them.
entries.variants: no one's /ˈnoʊ wʌnz/ · NO-wunz — the same pronoun written as two words on the -one stem, identical in grammar, reference, and register, and the form most edited American prose prefers in writing; ✗ noone's is not a spelling English uses, and ✗ none's does not exist at all. Also the else forms nobody else's and no one else's.
entries.see also: anyone's, everyone's, somebody's, somebody else's, nobody

entries.meaning: A possessive plus own, standing where a pronoun would — “the one belonging to that person and to nobody else.”
examples: Don't take an office pen — bring your own.
Everyone at the potluck brought their own.
What she wanted most was a room of her own. (the of-frame)
The city has a rhythm all its own — the standard repair for the missing standalone its.
My own is still in the shop, so I borrowed his. (subject, singular referent — is)
He finished the whole thing on his own. (fixed frame — “unaided”)
She held her own against three older players. (fixed frame — “kept up”)
✗ The choice is one's is not English; the repair is the choice is one's own.
entries.pronunciation note: the stress falls on own throughout the paradigm, and the possessive in front of it reduces — my own /mə ˈoʊn/, her own /ɚ ˈoʊn/, their own /ðɚ ˈoʊn/
entries.русский: свой собственный — подчёркивает исключительность: bring your own «приноси своё»
entries.register: neutral; the generic one's member of the paradigm is formal
entries.type: fused possessive — a possessive determiner plus the emphasizer own, standing where an independent possessive pronoun would
entries.person / number: any person and number — my own, your own, his own, her own, its own, our own, their own, generic one's own, regional y'all's own. One's own is the citation form, exactly as the reflexive of generic one is cited as oneself.
entries.refers to: whatever the possessive names, with own adding exclusivity — “belonging to that person and to nobody else.” The thing possessed is left to context: bring your own means your own drink, chair, lunch, or whatever the occasion supplies.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the understood possessed noun, not with the possessor: My own is still in the shop (one car), My own are still in the dryer (several shirts). Where an indefinite licenses it, the indefinite keeps its own singular verb and their own does not disturb it: ✓ Everyone brings their own, ✗ Everyone bring their own.
entries.pattern: [verb] [possessive] own — bring your own · [possessive] own [verb] — my own is in the shop · [determiner] [noun] of [possessive] own — a room of one's own, a place of his own · all [possessive] own — a rhythm all its own · on [possessive] own — she did it on her own · hold [possessive] own — he held his own · come into [possessive] own — the design came into its own
entries.contrast: With a noun after it (my own room, its own lease) the phrase is a determiner, and own itself is catalogued as an emphasizer in the determiner dictionary. Standing alone it is the pronoun — and it is the repair English uses for the two empty cells of the possessive paradigm: ✗ that collar is its becomes a life of its own, and ✗ the choice is one's becomes a room of one's own, which is why bare one's has no pronoun entry in this file at all. Against plain mine and yours: that's mine names the owner and stops there, that's my own insists nobody else has a share in it.
