entries.variants: my own, your own, his own, her own, its own, our own, their own, and regional y'all's own; generic one's own is the citation form. Informal speech also has me own, which is unstressed my rather than a separate word.
entries.see also: own (determiner), one's (determiner), its, mine, of mine (the double genitive)

entries.meaning: Names further people as possessors — “belonging to some other people.”
examples: He notices his own mistakes at once and others' not at all.
Our concerns are no different from others'. (comparison)
Half the coats were claimed by noon; the others' were still on the rack at closing. (with the article, plural referent — were)
The blame was partly mine and partly others'. (coordination)
It is easier to forgive one's own failures than others'.
Whose signatures are missing — ours, or others'? (question)
That opinion was never others' to give. (negative)
Three spellings, one sound: the others left early, at the other's expense, at others' expense.
entries.pronunciation note: the th is voiced; others, other's, and others' are one word in speech and three on paper
entries.русский: других, чужое — принадлежащее прочим людям; книжн., в речи чаще other people's
entries.register: neutral, and commoner in writing than in speech, where other people's usually takes its place
entries.type: plural indefinite genitive pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person plural — two or more further people. The singular of the same idea is another's. With the definite article, the others' names a specific remainder of a known group rather than an open set.
entries.refers to: people other than the ones already under discussion, human only. The thing possessed is understood from context, and is usually the noun that has just appeared: he sees his own faults quickly and others' slowly.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the understood possessed noun, never with the plural possessor: Others' are already in (several forms), Others' is the harder job (one job, though the possessors are many).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be others' — the harder work was others' · [possessive] and others' — his own and others' · the others' — the others' were still on the rack · comparison — no worse than others' · the determiner use, which belongs to the determiner dictionary — others' [noun] — at others' expense
entries.contrast: Three spellings, one sound. Others is the plain plural with no possession in it (the others left); other's is one further person's (at the other's expense); others' is several people's (at others' expense). Only the apostrophe separates them, and only in writing. Against another's, which is the singular. Against each other's and one another's, which are reciprocal: they read each other's drafts sends the reading crosswise inside the group, they read others' drafts sends it outside — catalogued in Reflexive and reciprocal pronouns.
entries.variants: the others', with the definite article, pointing at a specific remainder of a known group; other people's, the ordinary spoken equivalent; and the singular other's.
entries.see also: another's, somebody else's, the children's, each other's, others

entries.meaning: Names a possessor who is definitely not the person under discussion — “belonging to some other person.”
examples: This coat isn't mine — it must be somebody else's.
Half the luggage on the carousel turned out to be somebody else's.
The signature at the bottom was nobody else's but the director's.
He borrowed a jacket of somebody else's and never gave it back. (double genitive)
Whose turn is it? Not mine — somebody else's.
Is that phone yours or someone else's? (question)
Somebody else's is still sitting in the lost-and-found bin. (subject, singular verb — is)
entries.pronunciation note: the 's lands on else and is pronounced /ɪz/ after the /s/, exactly as in Chris's
entries.русский: чей-то другой, чужой — принадлежащий не тому, о ком речь
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: group genitive used as a pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular. The frame is productive: someone else's, anybody else's, everyone else's, nobody else's, who else's.
entries.refers to: an unnamed person other than the one already mentioned; human only. The thing possessed comes from context.
entries.agreement: grammatically singular: Somebody else's is missing. When the genitive heads a subject with its noun spelled out, the verb follows that noun instead — Somebody else's kids were in the pool.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be somebody else's · [noun] of somebody else's — a jacket of somebody else's · short answer — Not mine — somebody else's. · the frame — [indefinite pronoun] else's
entries.contrast: This is the clearest small proof that the English genitive attaches to a whole phrase, not to a word: else is not the possessor, but it ends the phrase, so it carries the ending. Hence ✓ somebody else's and ✗ somebody's else. The same mechanism gives ✓ who else's against the impossible ✗ whose else. Against each other's: somebody else's points outside the group, each other's points crosswise inside it.
entries.see also: somebody else's (determiner), somebody's, anyone's, nobody's, someone else's

entries.meaning: Names an unidentified possessor — “belonging to some person, and we don't know who.”
examples: That jacket on the chair is somebody's — don't throw it out. (subject complement)
Somebody's is missing from the pile; there are only nine. (subject, singular verb)
Whose keys are these? Somebody's, obviously. (short answer)
He turned up in a coat of somebody's that he'd found in the closet. (double genitive)
Is this bag yours, or someone's from the other table? (question, the -one stem)
That call wasn't mine to make — it was somebody's higher up. (negative)
Somebody's been in my office. (not the possessive — this is somebody has)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to the contraction somebody is; someone's /ˈsʌmwʌnz/ is the same pronoun on a different stem
entries.русский: чей-то — принадлежащий неизвестному лицу: «это чьё-то пальто»
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: indefinite genitive pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person singular. Someone's is the same word built on one; the else variant is somebody else's.
entries.refers to: one unidentified person — human only; the thing possessed is supplied by context (this coat is somebody's = somebody's coat). For a non-human possessor English uses a noun genitive instead (that collar is the dog's).
entries.agreement: grammatically singular, exactly like the pronoun it is built on — somebody is, ✗ somebody are: ✓ Somebody's is missing from the pile. Referring back to it, standard American English uses singular they, since the person's gender is unknown by definition: Somebody's phone is ringing, and they aren't answering it.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be somebody's — that jacket is somebody's · somebody's [verb] — somebody's is missing · [noun] of somebody's — a coat of somebody's · short answer — Whose is this? Somebody's, obviously. · the else variant — somebody else's
entries.contrast: Two words, one spelling: Somebody's at the door is somebody is, and Somebody's been in my office is somebody has, while this coat is somebody's is the possessive — expand it to test. Somebody's coat has a noun after it and is a determiner. Against anyone's: somebody's points at one particular person whose identity is unknown, anyone's at any person at all — the wallet is somebody's says it has an owner, the race is anyone's says it has none yet. Against nobody's, which denies an owner outright.
entries.see also: somebody else's, anyone's, everyone's, nobody's, somebody

entries.meaning: An irregular plural plus 's, standing alone for the possessive noun phrase — “the one, or the ones, belonging to the children.”
examples: The coats in the front hall are the children's.
Every bedroom upstairs is the children's.
That schedule isn't ours to set — it's the children's.
The children's is the small table by the window. (subject, singular referent — is)
The loudest voices in the room were the children's.
Which locker is the women's? (question, same irregular pattern)
He's an old teacher of the children's from the school downtown. (double genitive)
Our coats went on the hook next to the children's. (object of a preposition)
entries.pronunciation note: an irregular plural takes the ordinary /z/ of the singular genitive, because the plural is not built with -s in the first place
entries.русский: детей, детское — принадлежащее детям (неправильное мн. ч. + 's)
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: irregular plural genitive used as a pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person, plural possessor, with a noun whose plural is irregular — children, men, women, people, mice.
entries.refers to: something belonging to the group named. The thing possessed is understood from context.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the understood possessed noun, not with the plural possessor: The children's are in the hall (several coats), The children's is the small table (one table).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be the children's · the children's be [complement] · the frame — [irregular plural]'s — the men's, the women's, the people's
entries.contrast: Where the apostrophe goes depends on how the plural is built. A regular plural already ends in -s, so the apostrophe follows it (the students', the Smiths'); an irregular plural does not, so it takes a full 's (the children's, the women's). Hence ✓ the children's and ✗ the childrens' — an apostrophe standing after the -s marks a plural genitive, so the second presupposes a plural ✗ childrens, and children is already the plural. The rule is mechanical: pluralize first, then add the apostrophe where the plural leaves off.
entries.see also: the Smiths', the company's, the children's (determiner), s' (plural genitive)

entries.meaning: An institution's name or description plus 's, standing alone — “the one belonging to the company.”
examples: The parking lot is the company's, not the city's.
Half the patents are the company's.
That call was the board's, not the company's.
The liability here is the company's alone.
Our margins are thin, but they're still better than the company's down the street. (the repair for ✗ than its)
Is the software the company's or the contractor's? (question)
The company's was the only bid that came in under budget.
entries.pronunciation note: the company's, the companies, and the companies' are all pronounced /ˈkʌmpəniz/ — the difference exists only on paper
entries.русский: компании — принадлежащее организации; заменяет отсутствующее самостоятельное its
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: genitive noun phrase used as a pronoun (fused genitive); institutional possessor
entries.person / number: third person; an organization treated as a singular possessor in American usage — the company … its, not their. British usage often takes such collectives as plural.
entries.refers to: an organization, agency, team, or other collective body. This is also the standard repair for the missing standalone its: where ✗ higher than its fails, higher than the company's works.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the understood possessed noun: The company's is the bigger stake (one stake), The company's are the white trucks (several). The possessor itself, being singular in American usage, pairs with its and with a singular verb: The company has raised its offer.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be the company's · the company's be [complement] · comparison — higher than the company's · the frame — the [institution]'s — the board's, the city's, the university's
entries.contrast: Three spellings, one pronunciation: the company's (one company owns it), the companies (plain plural, no possession), the companies' (several companies own it). Only the apostrophe tells them apart, and only in writing. Against its: the company's is what English uses when it needs a standalone third-person non-personal possessive, because the pronoun slot is empty.
entries.see also: the company's (determiner), its, John's, the children's

entries.meaning: A plural family name plus the plural apostrophe, standing alone — “the one, or the ones, belonging to the Smiths.”
examples: The house with the red door is the Smiths'.
That mail is the Smiths' — it landed in our box again.
Our yard ends at the fence; everything past it is the Smiths'.
The Smiths' is the only house on the block with a porch swing. (subject, singular referent — is)
The lawn mower isn't ours; it's the neighbors'. (negative)
Which boat is the Joneses'? (question — a name ending in a sibilant)
Our driveway is narrower than the Smiths'. (comparison)
She's a cousin of the Smiths' from out of state. (double genitive)
entries.pronunciation note: the plural genitive adds nothing you can hear — the Smiths, ✗ the Smith's, and the Smiths' are pronounced alike
entries.русский: Смитов — принадлежащее семье Смитов (мн. ч. + апостроф без s)
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: regular plural genitive used as a pronoun (fused genitive)
entries.person / number: third person, plural possessor — a family, a couple, a group named collectively.
entries.refers to: something belonging to the named group. The thing possessed is understood from context.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the understood possessed noun, never with the plural possessor: The Smiths' is the house with the red door — one house, singular verb, though the possessor is a whole family.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be the Smiths' · the Smiths' be [complement] · the frame — the [family name + plural]' — the Joneses', the Johnsons', the neighbors'
entries.contrast: Pluralize first, then add the apostrophe. The family is the Smiths, so the possessive is the Smiths' — ✗ the Smith's would mean one person named Smith. A name that already ends in a sibilant pluralizes with -es first: Jones → the Joneses → the Joneses'. And the plain plural takes no apostrophe at all: the holiday card is signed the Smiths, not ✗ the Smith's.
entries.see also: the children's, John's, s' (plural genitive), the company's

entries.meaning: A fixed coordination of pronoun and possessive — “you, and the people who belong to you.”
examples: Merry Christmas to you and yours.
You and yours are always welcome at our table. (plural verb — are)
Our thoughts are with you and yours this week. (condolence)
From me and mine to you and yours. (the first-person half of the frame)
Him and his cleared out two days before the storm hit. (object form frozen in subject position — informal)
She'd do anything for her and hers. (object of a preposition)
May the year be kind to you and yours. (toast)
The yours here means your family, not your belongings — compare Is this coat yours?, where it means the coat.
entries.pronunciation note: and reduces to /ən/ or to a syllabic /n̩/, and the phrase carries one stress, on yours
entries.русский: вы и ваши близкие — формула поздравлений; здесь yours = люди, а не вещи
entries.case: the first half takes whatever case the slot requires; the second is possessive
entries.register: neutral and formulaic. Holiday cards, toasts, condolences, and the closing lines of letters are where it lives; outside those it sounds deliberately warm.
entries.type: fixed coordination — a personal pronoun plus an elliptical genitive, filling one noun-phrase slot between them
entries.person / number: second person here, singular or plural addressee. The frame runs through the whole paradigm — me and mine, him and his, her and hers, us and ours, them and theirs — and whatever the person, the phrase as a whole is plural.
entries.refers to: the person addressed together with the people belonging to them — family, household, dependents. This is the one place in the file where yours means people rather than possessions: you and yours is not “you and your things.”
entries.agreement: plural, always: ✓ You and yours are in our thoughts, ✗ You and yours is in our thoughts. The coordination has two heads and the second is understood as a plural noun (your family), so no singular reading is available even when one person is being addressed.
entries.pattern: to you and yours — best wishes to you and yours · you and yours [plural verb] — you and yours are welcome · from me and mine to you and yours · [preposition] [pronoun] and [possessive] — she'd do anything for her and hers
entries.contrast: In me and mine and him and his the first half is the object form even when the phrase is the subject — Me and mine are fine — and that is a frozen idiom rather than the ordinary coordination error: the deletion test that condemns ✗ Me and him went has nothing to bite on here, because I and mine is not what anyone says either. It is still informal, and edited prose writes my family and I. Note also that yours in this phrase is the elliptical genitive with a human head understood — the same machinery as the children's — which is why you and yours means people while is this yours? means a coat.
entries.variants: me and mine, him and his, her and hers, us and ours, them and theirs; the archaic thee and thine; and the expanded you and all yours.
entries.see also: yours, mine, theirs, the children's, you

entries.meaning: Asks, or states, who the possessor is, with the thing possessed already understood from context.
examples: Whose is this? (interrogative pronoun — nothing follows it)
Whose are these gloves on the counter? (plural referent — are)
I found a badge in the parking lot, but I have no idea whose it is.
Nobody could remember whose the idea had been originally.
✓ Whose signature is missing? — determiner, because a noun follows; the pronoun is the bare Whose is missing?
It's an old house whose wiring needs replacing. (relative with a non-human antecedent — standard, despite the folk rule against it)
Half the coats were left unclaimed, and no one could say whose. (bare pronoun as the whole object of say)
Whether we send it back depends on whose it turns out to be. (fused relative as object of the preposition on)
✗ Whose else is it? → ✓ Who else's is it?

body: Interrogative pronoun — asks which person something belongs to, with no noun following: Whose is this? 2. Fused relative — introduces a clause that supplies its own antecedent: I don't know whose it is.
examples: Whose is this? (interrogative pronoun — nothing follows it)
Whose are these gloves on the counter? (plural referent — are)
I found a badge in the parking lot, but I have no idea whose it is.
Nobody could remember whose the idea had been originally.
✓ Whose signature is missing? — determiner, because a noun follows; the pronoun is the bare Whose is missing?
It's an old house whose wiring needs replacing. (relative with a non-human antecedent — standard, despite the folk rule against it)
Half the coats were left unclaimed, and no one could say whose. (bare pronoun as the whole object of say)
Whether we send it back depends on whose it turns out to be. (fused relative as object of the preposition on)
✗ Whose else is it? → ✓ Who else's is it?

entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; identical to who's
entries.русский: чей, чьего — вопросительное и относительное; и о людях, и о предметах
entries.register: neutral
entries.type: interrogative and relative pronoun (genitive)
entries.person / number: any person or number. It asks about, or refers to, a possessor without specifying one.
entries.refers to: both people and things. Whose is the only genitive relative English has, so it does duty for who and for which alike: the engineer whose design won, a novel whose ending nobody likes. Set against the rest of the family — who takes people, which takes things, that takes both — whose patterns with that: it takes both, and always has. The claim that whose may not have an inanimate antecedent is an invented rule; the alternative, of which, is grammatical but stiff (a novel the ending of which nobody likes). As a standalone pronoun the possessor is normally human.
entries.agreement: takes no agreement of its own. In a question the verb agrees with the noun that follows is/are: Whose is this? (one thing), Whose are these? (several). In a relative clause the verb agrees with the clause's own subject, not with whose.
entries.pattern: Whose is/are [noun phrase]? — Whose is this? · [verb] whose [clause] — I know whose it is · [preposition] whose [clause] — it depends on whose it is · the determiner use, which lives in the determiner dictionary — whose [noun] — whose car is that?
entries.contrast: Whose versus who's. Whose asks or states possession; who's is the contraction of who is or who has. Expand it: Who's calling? is who is calling, but Whose call is it? has no expansion, so it takes whose. Against which: which picks an item out of a set (Which is yours?), whose asks who owns it (Whose is this?). Against whom: whom is the object form of who, not a possessive — ✓ the client to whom I sent it, ✓ the client whose file I sent; in American English whom survives mainly right after a preposition, and elsewhere who is standard. Note also the impossible ✗ whose else — the phrasal genitive requires who else's.
entries.see also: who's (not a possessive pronoun), whose (determiner), whosever, who, whom, of which

entries.meaning: Introduces a clause that identifies a possessor without naming one, with the -soever of whatsoever on the end — “whoever's it may turn out to be.”
examples: Whosesoever it is, it cannot stay in the hallway. (the bare pronoun)
Whosesoever these are needs to claim them by Friday. (bare pronoun, plural referent inside the clause — singular main verb needs)
I'll hand the wallet over to whosesoever it turns out to be. (object of a preposition)
Whose soever sins ye remit, they are remitted unto them. (John 20:23, King James Version — the split spelling)
Whosesoever name is on the deed will have to sign it. (determiner use inside the clause)
Said plainly today: Whoever's it is should say so now.
The suffix is the one in whatsoever, which is the only member of the family still in ordinary use: no doubt whatsoever.
entries.pronunciation note: four syllables, main stress on -ev-; no weak form, and no modern speaker has occasion to reduce it
entries.русский: чей бы то ни было — устар., книжн. (библейский стиль); сам себе антецедент
entries.register: archaic and formal. The King James Bible, older legal drafting, and deliberate period style. An American who meets this word meets it in John 20:23 or in a document written to sound like it.
entries.type: fused relative pronoun (genitive) — whose plus the emphatic suffix -soever; catalogued here for the standalone use, the prenominal use being a determiner
entries.person / number: third person singular. It names one possessor, whatever the number of the things involved.
entries.refers to: a human possessor whose identity is unknown or deliberately left open — “whoever's, no matter whose.” Like whosever, it supplies its own antecedent, so no noun stands in front of it.
entries.agreement: the free relative names one person, so the main verb is singular even when a plural noun sits beside it: ✓ Whosesoever these are needs to claim them. The plural noun inside the clause takes its own plural verb (these are), and that has no effect on the main one.
entries.pattern: Whosesoever it is, [main clause] — whosesoever it is, it has to move · [preposition] whosesoever [clause] — give it back to whosesoever it is · the King James spelling, split around the noun — whose soever [noun] · the prenominal frame, which is the determiner — whosesoever [noun] [verb]
entries.contrast: -soever is an intensifying suffix meaning “at all, no matter which,” the same one in whatsoever, whosoever, wheresoever, whensoever, and howsoever. Only whatsoever survives in ordinary American English, and chiefly in negatives (no doubt whatsoever); the rest, this one included, are archaic. Against whosever, which is merely rare and bookish rather than archaic, and against whoever's, which is what an American actually says. Note that the King James text splits the word around its noun — Whose soever sins ye remit — where modern printings close it up.
entries.variants: whose soever, the split King James spelling; whosoever's; and the archaic whoseever. The everyday equivalent is whoever's.
entries.see also: whosever, whose, whosever (determiner), who

entries.meaning: Introduces a clause that identifies a possessor without naming one — “the person whose.”
examples: Whosever it is, it can't stay in the hallway. (the bare pronoun — the standalone use catalogued here)
Whosever these are, they need to be off the counter by noon. (bare pronoun, plural referent inside — are)
I'll give the wallet back to whosever it turns out to be. (object of a preposition)
Whoever's it is should say so now. (the ordinary spoken standalone form)
Whosever keys these are needs to come get them. (determiner inside the clause — note the plural noun beside it and the singular main verb needs)
Whosever car is blocking the driveway needs to move it. (determiner use, catalogued in the determiner dictionary)
Whoever's umbrella this is, they left it in the rain. (the spoken determiner form; singular they refers back to the unknown owner)
Leave the box at the desk and whosever it is can pick it up. (bare pronoun heading the subject of the second clause)
She'll hand the badge over to whosever it proves to be. (bare pronoun after a preposition)
entries.pronunciation note: no weak form; the everyday spoken equivalent is whoever's /huˈɛvɚz/
entries.русский: того, чей — книжн., редк.: «тот, чей»; существительное перед ним не нужно
entries.register: formal, rare — it sounds bookish in speech
entries.type: fused relative pronoun (genitive) — catalogued here for the standalone use, since the commoner prenominal use (whosever car…) is a determiner and belongs to the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: third person singular. It names one possessor, whatever the number of the things involved.
entries.refers to: a human possessor whose identity is unknown or beside the point. Unlike whose, it supplies its own antecedent — whosever means “the person whose,” so no noun precedes it.
entries.agreement: the free relative names one person, so the main verb is singular even when a plural noun sits next to it: ✓ Whosever keys these are needs to claim them. Many speakers say need by attraction to keys; a careful editor will change it back.
entries.pattern: standalone, the pronoun use — Whosever it is, [main clause]: Whosever it is, it needs to move · [preposition] whosever [clause] — give it back to whosever it is · everyday spoken standalone — whoever's it is · the prenominal frame, which is the determiner and lives in the other dictionary — whosever [noun] [verb] …
entries.contrast: In American speech people say whoever's: Whoever's car that is needs to move it. Whosever is the tidy written form and rare enough to sound stilted; whosesoever and whoseever are archaic. Do not confuse it with relative whose, which needs an antecedent in front of it (the man whose car…) where whosever contains its own (whosever car…). Note too that whoever's is ambiguous on paper — it is also the contraction of whoever is (Whoever's driving should stop).
entries.see also: whose, whosever (determiner), who's (not a possessive pronoun), who

entries.meaning: Dialectal possessive pronouns matching his, hers, ours, yours, theirs, formed on the pattern of mine and thine.
examples: That truck out front is hisn.
Ourn is the blue house at the end of the lane.
Is this coat yourn or mine?
The bottom field used to be theirn before the road went through.
She said the recipe was hern, handed down from her grandmother.
✗ Hisn truck is in the shop. → ✓ His truck is in the shop. (the form never precedes a noun, even in the dialects that use it)
entries.pronunciation note: also written with an apostrophe — his'n, her'n, our'n, your'n, their'n
entries.русский: его, её, наш, ваш, их — диал., нестанд.: Аппалачи, Озарк, Юг и Мидленд США
entries.register: nonstandard. Appalachian, Ozark, and older Southern and Midland American speech, and the northern English dialects those came from. Unremarkable locally, strongly marked in writing, and never appropriate in edited prose.
entries.type: possessive pronouns, dialectal
entries.person / number: third singular masculine (hisn), third singular feminine (hern), first plural (ourn), second singular or plural (yourn), third plural (theirn). There is no ✗ minen — mine already ends in the -n these were built from.
entries.refers to: exactly what the standard forms refer to; the meaning is identical. Only the register differs.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the thing possessed, as with the standard forms: Ourn is the blue house, Ourn are in the barn.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be hisn — that truck is hisn · ourn [verb] — ourn is the blue house · ✗ hisn [noun] — impossible; these forms never precede a noun. The determiner in the same dialects is the ordinary his, her, our, your, their.
entries.contrast: They were built by analogy with mine and thine, which is why they end in -n, and they behave like mine: they stand alone and never precede a noun. ✓ That truck is his'n, ✗ his'n truck. The slot test settles it in one move. Against the standard forms, the only difference is register — a reader will place the speaker geographically and socially, which is exactly why the forms belong in dialogue and nowhere else.
entries.see also: mine, thine, his, theirs, mines

entries.meaning: A regularized form of mine, built by copying the -s of yours, hers, ours, and theirs.
examples: That seat is mines. (nonstandard; standard English is That seat is mine.)
Which one is mines? (nonstandard question form)
He said the jacket was mines, but I'd never seen it before.
Mines is the one on the end. (nonstandard subject use)
The logic behind it is plain: yours, hers, ours, theirs — so mines.
✓ In writing, always mine: That seat is mine.
entries.pronunciation note: an added /z/ on the standard mine
entries.русский: моё — нестанд.: вариант mine в афроамериканском английском; на письме ошибка
entries.register: nonstandard. Common in African American English and in some urban and regional varieties, and ordinary within them; marked wrong by every editor and every standardized test. Do not use it in writing.
entries.type: possessive pronoun, nonstandard
entries.person / number: first person singular — the same reference as mine, with no difference in meaning.
entries.refers to: something belonging to the speaker; identical in reference to mine.
entries.agreement: the verb still agrees with the thing possessed, not with the -s: That book is mines has a singular referent despite the ending, and speakers who use the form do not treat it as a plural.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be mines — that seat is mines · ✗ mines [noun] — the form never precedes a noun, exactly like mine
entries.contrast: The -s is regularization, not a plural: yours, hers, ours, theirs all end in -s, so mine gets one too. That makes the form perfectly logical and still nonstandard. Standard English is ✓ That's mine. Note the parallel with the dialectal -n forms, which regularize in the opposite direction, adding the ending of mine to his, her, our, your, their.
entries.see also: mine, hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn, yours, ours

entries.meaning: The possessive pronoun of the old familiar singular thou — “the one, or the ones, belonging to thee.”
examples: For thine is the kingdom, and the power, and the glory, for ever. (the Lord's Prayer, Matthew 6:13, King James Version)
Not my will, but thine, be done. (Luke 22:42, KJV)
All that I have is thine.
What's mine is thine, and what's thine is mine. (coordination)
He greeted an old friend of thine at the gate. (double genitive, Early Modern English)
✗ Thine sword is the standard beginner's error: sword begins with a consonant, and a noun follows, so the phrase is thy sword.
entries.pronunciation note: the word only ever turns up stressed
entries.русский: твоё — устар.: библейское и поэтическое; в современном языке yours
entries.register: archaic. The King James Bible, the Book of Common Prayer, Shakespeare, hymns, and deliberate period writing. A few conservative Quaker meetings still keep the plain speech (thee, thy, thine) as a religious practice; outside that, an American reads this word and never says it.
entries.type: possessive pronoun, archaic
entries.person / number: second person singular, familiar — the possessive pronoun matching thou and thee. A plural addressee took yours even in Early Modern English, which is the distinction modern your/yours lost.
entries.refers to: something belonging to one familiar addressee. In modern English the whole range is covered by yours.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the thing possessed: the kingdom is thine (singular), these are thine (plural).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be thine — the kingdom is thine · [noun] of thine — a friend of thine · coordination — what's mine is thine · the prenominal use, which is the determiner and lives in the determiner dictionary — thine eyes, thine own self
entries.contrast: Two words are spelled thine, and the usual test separates them: a noun after it makes it a determiner (thine eyes, and only before a vowel sound — thy sword before a consonant), nothing after it makes it a pronoun (the kingdom is thine). The first-person twin is mine, and the machinery is identical. The beginner's error is sprinkling thine on any noun to sound old: ✗ thine sword.
entries.see also: thine (determiner), thy (determiner), mine, yours, thou

entries.meaning: The Southern second-person plural possessive — “the one, or the ones, belonging to you all.”
examples: That truck in the driveway is y'all's.
Y'all's is the house with the blue shutters.
Is this cooler ours or y'all's? (question)
He's a cousin of y'all's on your mother's side. (double genitive)
The mess in the kitchen sure isn't mine — it's y'all's. (negative)
The whole back row is all y'all's. (emphatic plural)
entries.pronunciation note: also spelled y'alls, yall's, and ya'll's; the last of these puts the apostrophe in the wrong place, since the contraction is you all
entries.русский: ваш, ваше — разг., южн.-амер.: принадлежащее нескольким собеседникам
entries.register: regional and informal. Southern and South Midland American English, where it is entirely ordinary in speech, and increasingly heard nationally. Not used in formal writing.
entries.type: possessive pronoun, regional — the same form also serves as a determiner, which is catalogued in the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: second person plural — the plural your/yours that standard English lacks. Related forms: all y'all's (emphatic plural), and the northern equivalents you guys' and yinz's.
entries.refers to: something belonging to the people being addressed, two or more of them. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, or uncountable.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the thing possessed: Y'all's is the blue truck, Y'all's are in the cooler.
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be y'all's — that truck is y'all's · y'all's [verb] — y'all's is the blue one · [noun] of y'all's — a cousin of y'all's · emphatic — all y'all's · the determiner use, which belongs to the other dictionary — y'all's [noun]
entries.contrast: Unlike the standard possessives, y'all's is spelled with an apostrophe, because it is a genitive built on a contracted noun phrase (you all → y'all → y'all's), not one of the seven personal forms. It fills a real gap: standard yours cannot distinguish one addressee from several, and y'all's can. Against yours, the difference is register and number, not meaning.
entries.variants: all y'all's, the emphatic plural — the whole back row is all y'all's — which marks off the whole group addressed from a smaller one already mentioned; the spellings y'alls and yall's, and the misplaced apostrophe of ✗ ya'll's; the Northern equivalent you guys'; and Pittsburgh's yinz's.
entries.see also: yours, you guys', y'all's (determiner), hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn, you

entries.meaning: The Northern and general-American second-person plural possessive — “the one, or the ones, belonging to you guys.”
examples: Is this cooler ours or you guys'?
You guys' is the blue tent at the end of the row. (subject, singular referent — is)
The seats in the back row are you guys'. (plural referent)
He's an old friend of you guys' from college. (double genitive)
The mess in the kitchen sure isn't mine — it's you guys'. (negative)
Most speakers say it with the extra syllable: That car is you guys's.
In the South the same sentence comes out That car is y'all's. (the regional counterpart)
entries.pronunciation note: the plain possessive adds nothing you can hear — you guys and you guys' are identical in speech — which is why many speakers pronounce the ending out as you guys's
entries.русский: ваш, ваше — разг.: то же о нескольких собеседниках, общеамериканский вариант
entries.register: informal. The Northern, Western, and general-American answer to Southern y'all's: ordinary in speech across most of the country, and almost never written — partly because it is informal, partly because nobody agrees how to spell it.
entries.type: possessive pronoun, regional and informal — the same form serves as a determiner, catalogued in the determiner dictionary
entries.person / number: second person plural — the plural your/yours that standard English lacks. You guys is addressed to groups of any gender in most of the country, though some speakers avoid it for an all-female group and reach for you all instead.
entries.refers to: something belonging to the people being addressed, two or more of them. The thing possessed may be singular, plural, or uncountable.
entries.agreement: the verb agrees with the thing possessed, not with the plural addressee: You guys' is the blue tent (one tent), You guys' are in the back seat (several).
entries.pattern: [noun phrase] be you guys' — that cooler is you guys' · you guys' [verb] — you guys' is the blue one · [noun] of you guys' — a friend of you guys' · the pronounced-out genitive — you guys's · the determiner use, which belongs to the other dictionary — you guys' [noun] — you guys' car
entries.contrast: The spelling is the whole difficulty, and it is unsettled: you guys', you guys's, and you guyses are all written, because the ending is landing on a phrase whose last word already ends in /z/ — the same collision that produces the Joneses'. Southern y'all's has no such problem, which is one reason it travels better into print. Against yours the difference is number and register: yours cannot tell one addressee from several, and this can. Note that guys here has been bleached of its noun meaning entirely — you guys' is a second-person plural pronoun, takes no article, and says nothing about anyone's gender.
entries.variants: you guys's (the pronounced-out genitive, /ju ˈɡaɪzɪz/) and you guyses; youse guys' and yous guys' (New York, New Jersey, Philadelphia); yinz's (Pittsburgh); you-uns' and you'uns' (Appalachian); and the Southern y'all's and all y'all's.
entries.see also: y'all's, yours, hisn, hern, ourn, yourn, theirn, y'all's (determiner), you

entries.ipa: pronounced exactly like hers, ours, yours, theirs, its
entries.meaning: The apostrophe errors that the possessive pronouns attract — listed here only so they can be recognized and removed.
examples: ✗ She's a friend of her's. → ✓ She's a friend of hers.
✗ The blue house is our's. → ✓ The blue house is ours.
✗ Is this seat your's? → ✓ Is this seat yours?
✗ The mistake was their's. → ✓ The mistake was theirs.
✗ The dog hurt its' paw. → ✓ The dog hurt its paw.
The one apostrophe that is correct here belongs to the noun genitives: ✓ the coat is John's, ✓ the coats are the children's.
entries.pronunciation note: the misspellings are inaudible — they exist only in writing
entries.русский: орфографическая ошибка — эти местоимения никогда не пишутся с апострофом
entries.case: none — a misspelling carries no case of its own; the forms these misspell are possessive
entries.register: always an error
entries.type: misspellings — not words in any variety of English
entries.person / number: not applicable.
entries.refers to: nothing. These are the correct pronouns with an apostrophe wrongly inserted.
entries.agreement: not applicable.
entries.pattern: ✗ a friend of her's → ✓ of hers · ✗ the house is our's → ✓ is ours · ✗ is that your's? → ✓ yours · ✗ the fault was their's → ✓ theirs · ✗ its' tail → ✓ its tail
entries.contrast: The rule has no exceptions: personal possessive pronouns never take an apostrophe. Hers, ours, yours, theirs, its, and whose are all apostrophe-free. The error is understandable, because every other possessive in English is built with one — John's, the company's, somebody else's, the Smiths' — so the hand adds it out of habit. The one to single out is ✗ its', which is not a possible English word in any sense: there is no reading, no dialect, and no register that calls for it.
entries.see also: hers, ours, yours, theirs, it's (not a possessive pronoun)

entries.meaning: The contraction of it is or it has — a possessive-shaped trap with no possessive function whatsoever.
examples: It's going to rain all weekend.
It's been three years since we moved. (it has)
I think it's your turn.
It's not the money, it's the principle. (negative)
Do you think it's too late to call? (question — and the test still works: do you think it is too late)
If it's broken, its warranty should cover the repair. (both words, one sentence)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to its; the two are distinguishable only in writing
entries.русский: это, оно есть — сокращение it is / it has; притяжательное — its, без апострофа
entries.case: none — it is a subject plus a verb
entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing; spelled out in the most formal prose
entries.type: contraction of it is or it has
entries.person / number: third person singular, non-personal — but as a subject and a verb, not as a possessive.
entries.refers to: nothing possessively. The it inside it is the ordinary dummy or referential subject pronoun.
entries.agreement: it is the agreement — the contracted verb is already third-person singular: It's raining, It's been a week.
entries.pattern: It's [adjective] — It's cold. · It's [noun phrase] — It's a shame. · It's [verb]-ing — It's raining. · It's been [noun phrase] — It's been a week.
entries.contrast: ✗ The dog hurt it's paw → ✓ its paw: expand it and the dog hurt it is paw is nonsense, so the possessive is required. In the other direction, ✗ Its raining → ✓ It's raining. This is the most-corrected error in written English, and the test takes one second. And ✗ its' is not a word in any sense at all.
entries.see also: its, who's (not a possessive pronoun), you're (not a possessive pronoun), it's (determiner dictionary)

entries.meaning: The contraction of existential or locative there with is or has — a homophone of theirs with no possessive meaning at all.
examples: There's a problem with the second invoice.
There's been a mistake. (there has)
There's nothing left in the fridge. (negative)
There's three people ahead of us. (ordinary speech; formal writing takes There are three people)
✗ The blue car is there's. → ✓ The blue car is theirs.
There's their car, and the one behind it is theirs too. (all three words, one sentence)
entries.pronunciation note: homophonous with theirs in ordinary American speech
entries.русский: есть, имеется — сокращение there is / there has; не притяжательное
entries.case: none — it is a dummy subject plus a verb
entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing
entries.type: contraction of there is or there has
entries.person / number: not applicable. The there inside it is the existential dummy subject, which carries no person or number of its own.
entries.refers to: nothing. Existential there points at nothing at all; it fills the subject slot that English grammar requires.
entries.agreement: this is where it bites. Existential there takes its number from the noun that follows the verb, not from there: ✓ There is one problem, ✓ There are three problems. Spoken American English uses there's with plurals constantly (there's two people here), at every level of education and formality; in edited prose it is still changed to there are.
entries.pattern: There's [singular noun phrase] — There's a problem. · There's been [noun phrase] — There's been a mistake. · formal plural — There are [plural noun phrase] · ✗ there's used possessively — impossible
entries.contrast: Two spellings share this sound, and two more only look as though they do. There's (there is/has) and theirs, the possessive pronoun (the car is theirs), are the true homophones, both /ðɛrz/. They're (they are) and plain there (the place word or the dummy subject) are /ðɛr/ — they lack the final /z/ altogether, so they sound like their, not like this word. Expand the contraction to test: if there is fits, the apostrophe belongs. ✗ The car is there's is one of the more common possessive errors in casual writing.
entries.see also: theirs, they're (not a possessive pronoun), it's (not a possessive pronoun)

entries.meaning: The contraction of they are — a homophone of their and there, and no kind of possessive.
examples: They're running twenty minutes behind.
They're the ones who called about the apartment.
They're not going to make the deadline. (negative)
✗ They're car is blocking the driveway. → ✓ Their car is blocking the driveway.
They're over there, and the blue one is theirs. (all three words, one sentence)
Somebody left a bag; they're going to want it back, and it's probably theirs. (singular they, standard)
entries.pronunciation note: homophonous with their and with there
entries.русский: они есть — сокращение they are; притяжательные — their, theirs
entries.case: none — it is a subject plus a verb
entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing
entries.type: contraction of they are
entries.person / number: third person plural, or singular they.
entries.refers to: whatever they refers to — but as a subject, not as a possessor.
entries.agreement: it is the agreement: the contracted verb is plural are, and it stays are with singular they as well (They're the applicant who called).
entries.pattern: They're [adjective] — They're late. · They're [noun phrase] — They're the ones who called. · They're [verb]-ing — They're leaving. · ✗ they're [noun] — impossible; the determiner is their
entries.contrast: The classic three-way pileup is their (the possessive determiner — their car), there (the place word or dummy subject), and they're (they are) — three spellings, one sound, /ðɛr/. Theirs, the possessive pronoun (the car is theirs), is a fourth spelling in the same family, but it is not a homophone of these three: it carries a final /z/ and pairs by sound with there's instead. Expand it: ✗ they're car becomes they are car, which is nonsense, so the determiner their is required.
entries.see also: theirs, there's (not a possessive pronoun), their (determiner), they

entries.meaning: The contraction of who is or who has — a homophone of whose with no possessive function.
examples: Who's calling, please?
Who's been using my charger? (who has)
She's the one who's in charge of scheduling. (relative clause)
Who's not on the list yet? (negative)
✗ Who's keys are these? → ✓ Whose keys are these?
Who's the owner, and whose is the truck out front? (both words, one sentence)
entries.pronunciation note: identical to whose
entries.русский: кто есть — сокращение who is / who has; притяжательное — whose
entries.case: none — it is a subject plus a verb
entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing
entries.type: contraction of who is or who has
entries.person / number: any person or number; the verb inside it is third-person singular is or has.
entries.refers to: a person, as the subject of a clause — never as a possessor.
entries.agreement: it is the agreement: Who's coming? is singular by default even when the answer is plural (Who's coming? — The Smiths are). Where a plural subject is explicit, use who are: Who are these people?
entries.pattern: Who's [verb]-ing? — Who's calling? · Who's [noun phrase]? — Who's the manager? · Who's been [verb]-en? — Who's been here? · relative — the one who's in charge
entries.contrast: ✗ Who's turn is it? → ✓ Whose turn is it?: expand it and who is turn is nonsense, so the possessive is required. In the other direction, ✗ Whose calling? → ✓ Who's calling? The test is the same one that settles its/it's and your/you're.
entries.see also: whose, who, it's (not a possessive pronoun), who's (determiner dictionary)

entries.meaning: The contraction of you are — a homophone of your with no possessive function.
examples: You're going to want a jacket.
You're the only one who answered.
You're not on the list. (negative)
✗ Your welcome. → ✓ You're welcome.
✗ You're seat is in the back row. → ✓ Your seat is in the back row.
You're early, your badge is at the desk, and the blue folder is yours. (all three words, one sentence)
entries.pronunciation note: in ordinary speech the weak /jɚ/ is identical to weak your, which is exactly why the two get swapped in writing
entries.русский: ты, вы есть — сокращение you are; притяжательные — your, yours
entries.case: none — it is a subject plus a verb
entries.register: neutral in speech and ordinary writing
entries.type: contraction of you are
entries.person / number: second person, singular or plural.
entries.refers to: the addressee, as the subject of a clause — never as a possessor.
entries.agreement: it is the agreement: you are is invariably plural in form, for one addressee or many (You're late, said to one person or to six).
entries.pattern: You're [adjective] — You're right. · You're [noun phrase] — You're the manager. · You're [verb]-ing — You're leaving already? · ✗ you're [noun] — impossible; the determiner is your
entries.contrast: ✗ You're seat is in the back → ✓ Your seat: expand it and you are seat is nonsense. In the other direction, ✗ Your welcome → ✓ You're welcome, which is the single most common form of this error. Note that the possessive pronoun is yours, with no apostrophe at all: ✓ the seat is yours, ✗ your's.
entries.see also: yours, your (determiner), it's (not a possessive pronoun), you
